summary: Live Science recaps ten notable solar discoveries of 2023, including a stronger-than-forecast solar maximum arriving by 2024, a slightly smaller corona, auroras on the sun, and evidence of an ancient Miyake Event. It also covers superflares as a possible spark for life, neutrinos as a clue to dark matter, shorter past solar cycles, the heartbeat-signal puzzle, coronal rain and picojets.
one_line: A roundup of ten major 2023 findings about the sun, from an imminent explosive solar maximum to solar auroras, superflares and picojets.
key_facts: The current solar cycle began in 2019; early forecasts said the solar maximum would arrive from 2025 onward and be relatively weak.
Live Science's June feature said the solar maximum would likely arrive by 2024 and be more active than forecast; an updated forecast in October was more in line with that.
A November study found the sun is likely between 0.03% and 0.07% smaller than thought, because waves traveling through the corona do not reach as far as expected.
A November study detected radio bursts above a sunspot with frequencies similar to Earth's auroras, suggesting the sun has auroras, likely caused by electrons accelerated along magnetic field lines.
In October, researchers reported a Miyake Event about 14,000 years ago, found in fossilized tree rings unearthed in the French Alps, possibly the most powerful solar outburst ever to hit Earth.
A May study fired charged particles at a lab-recreated early atmosphere and produced amino acids and carboxylic acids, suggesting superflares could have sparked life on Earth.
The researchers argue lightning would not have provided nearly as much power as superflares for kickstarting life.
An August pre-print suggested the sun's core may hold concentrated dark matter that would emit slightly extra neutrinos; these extra neutrinos have not been detected so far.
A June pre-print using ancient Korean texts on auroras during the Maunder Minimum (1645–1715) suggests solar cycles then lasted only eight years, versus about 11 years now.
Scientists traced heartbeat-like quasi-periodic pulsations in solar radio bursts, studied in a 2017 solar flare, to fluctuations in electrical current fields across plasma loops.
In July, scientists announced coronal rain, clumps of cooler, denser plasma up to 435 miles (700 kilometers) across falling along magnetic field lines, described as shooting stars.
In August, the European Space Agency's Solar Orbiter spotted picojets from coronal holes, which may provide the energy to trigger gusts of solar wind.
